extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and mathematicians interested in the history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Write or evaluate a historical/encyclopedic account of a major mathematical theorem (here: Fermat's Last Theorem), emphasizing statements of results, major attempts, errors, key ideas, and final resolution. The page summarizes historical progress, important contributors, methods, and the eventual proof and review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise statement of the theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermat's Last Theorem states that x^n + y^n = z^n has no non-zero integer solutions for x, y and z when n > 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical account should begin by giving the exact, unambiguous formulation of the theorem being discussed so readers know the precise object of study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an explicit proof, not just a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermat's marginal note 'I have discovered a truly remarkable proof which this margin is too small to contain.' illustrates that a claim without an explicit proof is unsatisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept bare assertions; include proofs or clear references to complete proofs. Highlight when a purported proof is only claimed (marginal note) and treat it skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous verification and detection of fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Euler claimed a proof for n = 3 but his proof contained a fallacy; later work must identify and correct such mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical accounts should note known fallacies, explain why an argument fails (e.g., invalid manipulation, unjustified assumptions), and describe how the error was or could be remedied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check validity of algebraic manipulations in the chosen number system
rubrics_metrics.description: Euler's method calculated with numbers of the form a + b√-3; these 'do not behave in the same way as the integers', a fact Euler failed to appreciate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proofs move from integers to algebraic integers or other number systems, explicitly verify that the properties (like unique factorization) used in the argument hold in that system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce composite exponents to prime exponents
rubrics_metrics.description: If n = p q, then a solution for exponent n gives a solution for exponent p by taking qth powers (i.e., reduce the problem to odd prime exponents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard reductions to simplify the problem; explain such reductions clearly so the reader understands why it suffices to consider prime exponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Split the problem into natural arithmetic cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophie Germain's work shows that under certain prime conditions one of x,y,z must be divisible by n, leading to Case 1 (none divisible) and Case 2 (exactly one divisible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline case distinctions (divisibility, parity, etc.), motivate focusing on particular cases, and explain how proofs treat each case separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate on the remaining hard cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical progress often involved proving easier subcases (e.g., n=3,4) and then concentrating on the remaining, harder cases (e.g., Case 2 for n=5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear which subcases were left after earlier work and why later efforts targeted those remaining difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure uniqueness of factorization or provide alternative theory when it fails
rubrics_metrics.description: Lamé's factorization approach required uniqueness of factorisation in certain complex numbers; Liouville doubted this and Kummer showed uniqueness failed but could be 'recovered' via ideal complex numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume unique factorization without justification; if it fails, explain the substitute theory (e.g., Kummer's ideals) and how it restores the necessary structure for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce new mathematical tools when existing methods fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Lamé had to introduce completely new methods; Kummer introduced ideal complex numbers; later the Shimura–Taniyama–Weil conjecture and modularity methods were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical accounts should show how conceptual advances or new theories (ideal theory, modularity, elliptic curves) changed the landscape and enabled proofs that were previously out of reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arithmetic invariants to classify solvable cases (regular vs irregular primes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kummer defined a prime p as regular (so FLT is true for p) if p does not divide the numerator of certain Bernoulli numbers B_2, B_4, ..., B_{p-3}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain any arithmetic criteria used to separate cases (e.g., regularity via Bernoulli numbers), give definitions, and indicate which primes satisfy them and why that matters for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate computational verification from proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Computational checks (e.g., verifying no counterexample up to 4,000,000 by 1993) provide evidence but do not substitute for a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing large-scale computations, make clear their scope and limitations, and emphasize that finiteness or boundedness results are not substitutes for a general proof that the number of solutions is zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce problems to broader conjectures where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Frey and others showed that a counterexample to FLT would contradict the Shimura–Taniyama–Weil conjecture, linking FLT to modularity of elliptic curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how reframing a problem in a broader theoretical context (e.g., modularity, elliptic curves) can provide new avenues for proof; explain the logical implications of such reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: A correct proof withstands peer review and resolves discovered gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiles announced a proof in 1993 but withdrew the claim after problems emerged in review; collaborating with Taylor he fixed the remaining issues and completed the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives should recount the peer-review process: identify gaps found, explain how they were addressed, and document corrections and final acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide complete calculations and explicit bounds where needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiles noted that the 'final calculation of a precise upper bound for the Selmer group ... is not yet complete' — such explicit calculations are necessary to complete reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof reduces the main statement to an explicit bound or calculation, include those computations or explain how and why they are carried out to completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute contributions and contextualize partial results
rubrics_metrics.description: The history records contributions by many mathematicians (Sophie Germain, Euler, Dirichlet, Lamé, Kummer, etc.), partial proofs for specific n, and the development of relevant theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good historical account identifies who proved what, for which cases, and how partial results fit together toward the final resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the persistence of false proofs and the need for scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem 'has the dubious distinction of being the theorem with the largest number of published false proofs' (e.g., over 1000 false proofs between 1908 and 1912).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize the importance of skepticism and careful checking in mathematical history; mention well-known false proofs as cautionary examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain significant conceptual advances and their mathematical impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Faltings' 1983 result (finiteness of coprime integer solutions for fixed n>2) represented a major conceptual step though it did not itself prove FLT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight major theorems that changed the problem's landscape, explain what they establish, and clarify why they were or were not sufficient to resolve the main question.
